title: Evaluation of Drought Prediction Performance in Indonesia Using Machine Learning
author: Kuswanto, Naufal

steps.title: Collect satellite and auxiliary datasets
steps.instruction: Download the TRMM precipitation product and the MERRA‑2 re‑analysis (including SSMI and TMI) for East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia; also obtain NDVI, average soil surface temperature (day and night), the Multivariate ENSO Index (MEI) and the Arctic Oscillation Index (AOI) for the same spatial grid.

steps.title: Calculate 3‑month SPI
steps.instruction: For each grid cell, compute the 3‑month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) from the TRMM and MERRA‑2 precipitation series; use the SPI as the drought‑status target variable.

steps.title: Assemble predictor matrix
steps.instruction: Create a table for every grid containing the predictors NDVI, average soil surface temperature (day), average soil surface temperature (night), MEI and AOI together with the corresponding 3‑month SPI class label.

steps.title: Configure 10‑fold cross‑validation
steps.instruction: Randomly split the full sample set of each grid into 10 equal parts (k = 10) and use each part once as the testing set while the remaining nine parts form the training set; repeat for all folds.

steps.title: Train and evaluate CART model
steps.instruction: For each grid cell, fit a Classification and Regression Tree (CART) on the training folds, prune the tree to the optimal complexity parameter (cp), and record accuracy and AUC on both training and testing folds.

substeps.instruction: Determine optimal cp by examining the complexity‑parameter plot; for the example grid (120.125°E, 8.625°S) the optimum cp = 0.0095.

The CART analysis is repeated independently for every grid; overall CART accuracy across all grids is reported above 80 % while AUC values range from 0.5 to 0.75.

steps.title: Train and evaluate Random Forest model
steps.instruction: For each grid cell, fit Random Forest classifiers using a grid of hyper‑parameters, evaluate with the same 10‑fold CV, select the best parameter set, and record accuracy and AUC.

substeps.instruction: Define hyper‑parameter ranges: mtree = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and ntry = 100, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000.
For each (mtree, ntry) pair, train the Random Forest on the training folds and compute the mean AUC over the 10 folds.
Select the pair with the highest mean AUC; for the example grid (120.125°E, 8.625°S) the optimal setting is mtree = 2 and ntry = 1500, giving an AUC = 0.6033.

The Random Forest analysis is repeated for all grids; overall average accuracy reaches ≈80 % and average AUC ≈0.6, notably higher than CART.

steps.title: Summarize and compare model performance
steps.instruction: Compile the per‑grid accuracy and AUC results for CART and Random Forest using both TRMM and MERRA‑2 datasets; generate plots of AUC distributions (e.g., Fig. 4 for CART and Fig. 6 for Random Forest) and report that MERRA‑2 together with Random Forest yields significantly higher AUC values (many grids > 0.8) than TRMM or CART.

description: Drought is a natural disaster of below-average precipitation in a certain area caused by disruption to an expected preciptation pattern, and it has a very wide impact. One type of drought that occurs in Indonesia is meteorological drought, which can be defined as an event that takes place naturally and repeatedly because of reduced rainfall from normal conditions [1]. One of the provinces in Indonesia with the most frequent meteorological droughts is East Nusa Tenggara (NTT), and this is listed as the top priority region that is most vulnerable to drought [2]. Mitigation of drought, by methods such as providing reliable predictions of future droughts, is definitely required to minimize the risk and the negative impact of drought. Meteorological drought monitoring can be done by examining the rainfall data recorded from observation stations [3]; such data are effective and relatively accurate in describing the rainfall in an area. However, meteorological stations are not evenly distributed, resulting in the reduced accuracy of the results of the analysis [4,5], particularly in regions with no stations. To deal with this drawback, a dataset of satellite-based data has been extensively used in many analyses [5]. Remote-sensing data originating from meteorological satellites can provide rainfall data with a better spatial and temporal distribution [6]. According to Rhee and Im [3], remote-sensing data can be used widely and dynamically in drought monitoring. For tropical regions, the remote-sensing data generated from meteorological satellites that have been widely used in various studies are from the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) [[7], [8], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]]. Most studies have found that TRMM satellite precipitation gives a relatively good performance. For the case of Indonesia, the performance of the TRMM has been investigated [16,17]. Hatmoko et al.
